title: Palpitations in a 66-year-old retired maintenance fitter
desc: This station is a focused palpitations history and examination of Frank, a 66-year-old retired maintenance fitter seeing his GP. For a couple of months he has had episodes of fluttering that start and stop suddenly, and they now happen every day. He has hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea, drinks about nine glasses of beer a day and smokes a pack a day. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, ECG and blood results, diagnoses paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, calculates his stroke risk, and outlines anticoagulation, rate control, investigations, risk factor management and safety netting.
focus: Palpitations: characterising the rhythm, screening cardiac, endocrine and psychiatric causes and AF risk factors, then diagnosing paroxysmal AF and planning stroke prevention and risk factor management
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a suburban general practice. Frank, a 66-year-old retired maintenance fitter, has booked an appointment because of palpitations. Your GP supervisor has asked you to see him first. A practice nurse is available, and the practice has a 12-lead ECG machine and an on-site pathology collection service.
tasks: Take a focused history from Frank and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Frank's observations, his 12-lead ECG and his blood results. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Frank, a 66-year-old retired maintenance fitter. You are a big man, sitting comfortably in the chair, a little anxious but chatty. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

Opening line: "It feels like my heartbeat is fluttering."

The palpitations (give only when asked):

  • If asked to expand: "It's just all over the place... sometimes it feels like my heart misses a beat and then other times it beats really fast."
  • If asked to tap it out: tap a fast, irregular beat on the desk, with no pattern to it.
  • Time course: "It's been happening for a couple of months now, but I can't really remember when it started. Comes and goes."
  • Onset and offset: the episodes start suddenly and stop suddenly.
  • Constant or episodic: episodic. If asked how long they last: anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours.
  • Frequency: they used to come every couple of days, but now they happen every day.
  • Today: if asked whether you have it now: "Yes, actually. It started again about 8.30 this morning while I was having a cup of tea."
  • Context: "When it happens I am not doing anything in particular. The last time it happened I was watching TV."
  • Better or worse: nothing makes it better or worse; the episodes stop by themselves.

Other symptoms (only if asked; all absent unless stated):

  • Heart: no chest pain, tightness or discomfort. No shortness of breath, no waking at night breathless, no needing extra pillows. No dizziness, light-headedness or fainting. No nausea, vomiting or sweating with the episodes. No ankle swelling. You feel a bit tired when an episode goes on for a while.
  • Thyroid: no weight loss (if anything you are gaining), no increased appetite, no heat intolerance, no shakiness, no diarrhoea, no neck swelling.
  • Mood and stress: you are stressed and worried about your wife, and your sleep has been broken since her diagnosis. You are not irritable or restless, and your concentration is fine.
  • Other triggers: no recent cough, fever or infection. No one has told you that you are anaemic. Two cups of coffee a day, no energy drinks, no recreational drugs. No cold and flu tablets or other over-the-counter medicines.
  • Stroke risk questions: no diabetes as far as you know, no stroke or "mini-stroke", no heart attack, angina or heart failure, no circulation problems in your legs.
  • Bleeding questions: no stomach ulcers, no bleeding problems, no blood in your stools or urine, no falls. You do not take aspirin or anti-inflammatories.

Past medical history:

  • High blood pressure for "about 10 years".
  • Sleep apnoea, diagnosed about 5 years ago. You use a CPAP machine most nights.
  • Appendix out at 19. No other operations.

Medicines: perindopril, one tablet in the morning (you are not sure of the dose). Nothing else.

Allergies: "Just hay fever." No medicine allergies.

Family history: your father died of a heart attack at 79. Your mother had "thyroid problems".

Social history:

  • Alcohol: about nine glasses of beer a day. If asked what size: middies of full-strength beer. You have never tried to cut down. Do not volunteer the amount; if asked in a non-judgemental way, answer honestly.
  • Smoking: a pack a day for about 30 years, and you still smoke.
  • Work: retired maintenance fitter.
  • Home: you live at home with your wife.
  • Stress: "My wife was recently diagnosed with bladder cancer, and it's been really stressful."
  • Exercise: "My weight stops me from doing exercise."
  • Diet: mostly takeaway or frozen meals.
  • Support: "I've got a good group of family and friends who check up on me often."

Ideas, concerns, expectations: "I think something is wrong with my heart." You are really worried because your father died of a heart attack, and you want to know whether you are going to have one. You hope the doctor can work out what is going on.

How Frank changes: if the candidate asks the nurse for an ECG, the nurse says "I'll do it now", and the examiner hands it over in Part 2. If the candidate is warm about your wife, you open up more. If they lecture you about the beer, you become defensive and give shorter answers.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: obese man, comfortable at rest, talking in full sentences. Not pale, not sweaty, not distressed. Smells of cigarette smoke. Weight 112 kg, height 176 cm (BMI 36.2 kg/m²).
  • Vital signs (09:20): radial pulse 108 beats/min, irregularly irregular, varying in volume. Apical rate counted over one minute 116 (a pulse deficit of 8). BP 148/88 mmHg. RR 16/min. SpO2 97% on room air. Temperature 36.8 °C.
  • Hands: tar staining of the right index and middle fingers. No tremor, no clubbing, no palmar erythema, no Dupuytren's contracture. Warm, capillary refill 2 seconds.
  • Face, eyes and neck: no exophthalmos, lid lag or lid retraction. No conjunctival pallor. No spider naevi. No goitre or thyroid nodules. JVP not raised. Carotids normal, no bruits.
  • Praecordium: apex beat difficult to feel because of body habitus, not obviously displaced. No heave or thrill. S1 of varying intensity, S2 normal. No murmurs (none in the mitral area in the left lateral position), no added sounds.
  • Chest: clear, no crackles or effusion.
  • Abdomen: obese, soft, non-tender. Liver edge not palpable. No ascites.
  • Legs: no pitting oedema. Calves soft and non-tender.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self (name and role), confirms Frank's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Uses plain language, acknowledges the stress of his wife's cancer, and asks about alcohol and smoking in a non-judgemental way.
History
Characterises the palpitations:
check.d: Tick each element of the presenting complaint covered.

kids.x: Establishes the rate and regularity of the palpitations (e.g. asks Frank to tap out the rhythm) and identifies them as fast and irregular.
kids.d: Credit tapping or explicit questioning about speed and regularity.

kids.x: Onset and offset (sudden), episodic, and how long episodes last (minutes to hours); finds he has one now.
Time course and frequency: a couple of months, from every couple of days to daily.
Context and modifying factors: at rest (watching TV), nothing helps, they stop by themselves.

check.x: Asks the cardiovascular cluster:

kids.x: Red flags: chest pain or tightness, breathlessness, dizziness or light-headedness, fainting (all absent).
kids.d: Fainting or near-fainting must be asked.

kids.x: Heart failure and other features: fatigue, orthopnoea, ankle swelling, nausea, sweating.

check.x: Uses cluster questions for other differentials and AF precipitants:
check.d: Tick each cluster asked; the cardiovascular cluster is marked in item 6.

kids.x: Thyroid: weight loss, increased appetite, heat intolerance, tremor or nervousness, sweating, diarrhoea, neck swelling.
Psychiatric: stress, worry, irritability, restlessness, sleep, concentration.
PIRATES precipitants: chest infection or sepsis, ischaemic or rheumatic heart disease, anaemia, alcohol, caffeine, drugs and stimulants.

check.x: Asks the history needed for stroke risk: heart failure, diabetes, previous stroke or TIA, and vascular disease (heart attack, peripheral arterial disease); all absent.
check.d: Hypertension is credited in item 10 and age is given in the stem. Credit if these conditions are asked about as part of the past medical history or the cardiovascular review.

check.x: Asks about bleeding risk before anticoagulation: previous bleeding or ulcers, aspirin or NSAIDs, falls.
Past medical history: hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea on CPAP (asks how often he uses it) and appendicectomy at 19.
Medicines (perindopril; no over-the-counter or stimulant products) and allergies (hay fever, no medicine allergies).
Family history: father died of a heart attack at 79, mother had thyroid problems.
Takes a social history:

kids.x: Quantifies alcohol: about nine glasses (middies of full-strength beer) a day.
Quantifies smoking: a pack a day for 30 years (about 30 pack-years), still smoking.
Stress (wife's bladder cancer), living situation and social support.
Exercise (limited by weight) and diet (takeaway and frozen meals).

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks something is wrong with his heart and fears a heart attack like his father's.
Examination
General inspection, weight and height (BMI 36.2), BP 148/88 and asks for RR, SpO2 and temperature.
Assesses the radial pulse over a full minute: 108, irregularly irregular, variable volume; counts the apical rate and finds a pulse deficit.
check.d: Recognising the irregularly irregular pulse is the critical element; the apex-radial deficit is supporting.

check.x: Looks for signs of thyrotoxicosis: tremor, eye signs (lid lag, exophthalmos) and goitre (none).
Examines the praecordium for structural heart disease: apex, heart sounds and murmurs, especially mitral (none).
Looks for heart failure: JVP, lung bases and peripheral oedema (none).
Looks for signs of chronic alcohol use and liver disease (palmar erythema, spider naevi, hepatomegaly; none).
Asks for a 12-lead ECG now, while Frank has symptoms.
Interpretation

Observations: HR 108 to 112 and irregular in the morning, BP not low (148/88, mildly raised) and SpO2 97%, so haemodynamically stable; by 15:45 a regular pulse of 76, suggesting the episode has ended by itself (paroxysmal); confirms with a repeat 12-lead ECG.

ECG: irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline, ventricular rate about 110: atrial fibrillation, new compared with the sinus rhythm 2 years ago; no ischaemic change.
check.d: Critical element: identifies atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular, no P waves). Comparison with the old ECG and absence of ischaemia are supporting.

check.x: Bloods: normal TSH and free T4 (thyroid excluded), normal Hb and white cells (anaemia and infection unlikely), low magnesium, normal potassium and calcium, eGFR 75; macrocytosis with raised GGT and transaminases fit heavy alcohol use.
check.d: Credit any three of these in the ISBAR or the diagnosis answer.

check.x: States the most likely diagnosis, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation, justified by the irregularly irregular rhythm and his risk factors (alcohol, smoking, hypertension, OSA, obesity, inactivity, stress).
Gives at least two differentials with a feature for or against (ectopic beats, atrial flutter or other SVT, thyrotoxicosis, anxiety, VT from ischaemic heart disease).
Calculates the stroke risk score: CHA2DS2-VA 2 (hypertension 1, age 65 to 74 1); CHA2DS2-VASc also 2.
Management
States that he is stable (no hypotension, chest pain, heart failure or syncope) and can be managed in general practice with the GP supervisor; names these features as reasons for ED.
Recommends oral anticoagulation with a DOAC (e.g. apixaban 5 mg twice daily) in preference to warfarin, and not aspirin.
check.d: Supporting, not required: eGFR/FBC/INR checked; bleeding risk addressed by reducing alcohol and controlling BP rather than withholding OAC.

check.x: Offers rate control for symptoms, such as a beta-blocker (metoprolol), titrated to symptoms and resting heart rate.
Arranges a transthoracic echocardiogram (LV function, valves, atrial size) and ambulatory ECG monitoring to measure the AF burden.
check.d: Credit if both the TTE and ambulatory ECG monitoring are named. Also credit a repeat ECG in sinus rhythm.

check.x: Manages AF risk factors:

kids.x: Advises reducing or stopping alcohol with support offered, and checks for dependence or withdrawal risk before advising abrupt cessation.
kids.d: Supporting, not required: thiamine; supported withdrawal plan or AOD referral if dependent.

kids.x: Weight loss (aim at least 10%) and graded physical activity.
BP control, nightly CPAP use and magnesium replacement.

check.x: Refers to a cardiologist to consider rhythm control (antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation) given daily symptomatic episodes.

Answers Frank in plain words: this is an irregular rhythm in the top chambers, not a heart attack; the main risk is stroke, which a blood thinner lowers; and smoking, alcohol, weight and BP still raise his heart attack risk.
check.d: Credit offering lipids and a cardiovascular risk assessment.

check.x: Safety netting
Gives stroke warning signs in plain words (face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech) and says to call 000 straight away.

Gives other red flags: chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, or palpitations with dizziness (call 000 or go to ED); and on a blood thinner, black stools, vomiting blood, blood in the urine or a head injury.
check.d: Credit if at least three specific red flags are named.

check.x: Arranges follow-up: GP review in 1 to 2 weeks with the echo and monitor results, a check of HR, BP and anticoagulant tolerance, the cardiology referral, and support for him as a carer.
check.d: Credit a GP review in 1 to 2 weeks plus any two of: echo/monitor results, HR and BP check, anticoagulant tolerance, cardiology referral, carer support.

part2.lead: It is now 15:45 the same day. Frank had his bloods taken this morning and has come back for his results. Here are his observations, the ECG the nurse recorded this morning and his blood results.
part2.patient:
Frank is present for question 4. His palpitations have stopped. When the candidate explains, he asks, if not already covered:

  • "Am I going to have a heart attack?"
  • "Do I really have to cut down the beer?"
  • "Isn't a blood thinner dangerous?"

He accepts the plan if it is explained kindly and he is offered help with the drinking. If he is lectured, he says, "It's the only thing keeping me sane with my wife being sick."

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse, seated, on room air.
handover.model:
Read: at 09:20 HR 108 irregular, BP 148/88, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C, alert, no pain. At 09:40 HR 112 irregular, BP 146/86. At 15:45 HR 76 regular, BP 142/84, RR 14, SpO2 97%.

For Frank: during the episode he had a moderately fast irregular pulse but a BP that was not low (mildly raised at 148/88), normal breathing and saturation and no chest pain, so he was haemodynamically stable. Nothing here needs an emergency response. The pulse became regular on its own by the afternoon, which suggests the episode stopped without treatment (paroxysmal); record a repeat 12-lead ECG now to confirm sinus rhythm.

What it changes: he can be managed in general practice. A regular pulse of about 75 can also be atrial flutter with 4:1 block, so palpation alone does not confirm the rhythm. The repeat ECG confirms sinus rhythm, checks the PR interval and looks for pre-excitation, and gives a baseline in sinus rhythm before any antiarrhythmic. Paroxysmal AF still carries a stroke risk, so stroke prevention is decided on his risk score, not on whether he is in AF now. His BP is a little high and needs control.

rows.note: Practice nurse on arrival: says the fluttering started at about 08:30
After the ECG; still feels the fluttering
Back for results: fluttering stopped by itself at about 11:30

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (09:35)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, recorded at 09:35 by the practice nurse while Frank had palpitations. Standard calibration (10 mm/mV, 25 mm/s).

  • Rate: ventricular rate about 110 beats/min (range 90 to 135).
  • Rhythm: irregularly irregular. No discernible P waves; fine irregular fibrillatory waves in the baseline, best seen in V1 and II. No regular flutter waves.
  • Axis: normal (+20°).
  • PR interval: not measurable.
  • QRS: 94 ms, narrow. No bundle branch block. No delta wave.
  • QT: QTc about 430 ms (averaged over several beats).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression, no T-wave inversion.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves. No left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage.
  • Comparison: ECG from 2 years ago (hypertension review): sinus rhythm at 72 beats/min, normal axis and intervals, no ST or T-wave changes.

Conclusion: Atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 110 beats/min; new compared with 2 years ago; no acute ischaemic change.
handover.model:
Read: irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm at about 110 beats/min with no P waves and a fibrillatory baseline, normal axis, narrow QRS, normal QTc, no ST or T-wave change, no Q waves, no LVH, no pre-excitation. Sinus rhythm 2 years ago.

For Frank: this is atrial fibrillation with a moderately rapid ventricular response, captured during his symptoms and matching the fast, irregular rhythm he tapped out. There are no regular sawtooth flutter waves (against atrial flutter) and no ischaemic change. The spontaneous return to a regular pulse suggests paroxysmal AF; a repeat ECG now should confirm sinus rhythm.

What it changes: the diagnosis is confirmed. Calculate his stroke risk, consider rate control, and arrange an echocardiogram to look for structural heart disease. Keep the tracing as his baseline.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 10:00 at the on-site collection service; urgent results phoned through at 15:00. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: Hb 148 with a raised MCV of 101; white cells and platelets normal. Sodium, potassium, urea and creatinine normal, eGFR 75. Corrected calcium and phosphate normal, magnesium low at 0.66. GGT 142, ALT 48 and AST 52 raised; bilirubin, ALP and albumin normal. TSH and free T4 normal. HbA1c 5.8%. INR 1.0.

For Frank: normal thyroid function excludes hyperthyroidism as the trigger (important with his mother's thyroid history). A normal Hb and white cell count make anaemia and sepsis unlikely. The low magnesium may contribute to the arrhythmia. Macrocytosis with a raised GGT and transaminases fits heavy alcohol use, which is a major reversible AF risk factor. No diabetes, so it adds nothing to his stroke score.

What it changes: replace the magnesium. An eGFR of 75 with a normal Hb, platelets and INR allows a standard-dose DOAC. The liver results add to the case for cutting down alcohol and are a baseline to repeat.

ask: You are now calling your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Frank, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Frank now, here in general practice, including any further investigations.
Frank asks you: "Am I going to have a heart attack?" Please answer him, then tell him what to watch for and what follow-up you will arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student. Frank, 66, retired maintenance fitter.
  • Situation: paroxysmal AF, newly diagnosed. Daily palpitations, now settled. Stable.
  • Background: 2 months of sudden-onset irregular palpitations, now daily. Hypertension on perindopril, OSA on CPAP. About 9 beers a day, 30 pack-years and still smoking, BMI 36, wife has cancer. No stroke, diabetes, heart failure or vascular disease.
  • Assessment: HR 108 to 112 irregular, BP 148/88, SpO2 97%; regular at 76 by 15:45. ECG: irregularly irregular narrow complex, no P waves, rate about 110, no ischaemia; sinus rhythm 2 years ago. TFTs, Hb, K and Ca normal; Mg 0.66 low; MCV, GGT and transaminases raised (alcohol); eGFR 75. CHA2DS2-VA 2.
  • Recommendation: repeat ECG to confirm sinus rhythm, start a DOAC, consider a beta-blocker, echo and Holter, alcohol and smoking support, cardiology referral.

Most likely: paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Fast, irregular palpitations with sudden onset and offset, an irregularly irregular pulse, an ECG with no P waves, and spontaneous return to a regular rhythm. Risk factors: alcohol, smoking, hypertension, OSA, obesity, inactivity, stress, age.

  • Atrial or ventricular ectopic beats: for: "misses a beat". Against: sustained fast episodes, and the ECG.
  • Atrial flutter or other SVT: for: sudden onset and offset. Against: irregular rhythm, no flutter waves.
  • Thyrotoxicosis: for: mother's thyroid history. Against: no symptoms, normal TFTs.
  • Anxiety: for: major stress. Against: objective AF on the ECG.
  • VT from ischaemic heart disease (must not miss): for: smoker, hypertensive. Against: narrow QRS, no chest pain or syncope.

1. Disposition: stable (no hypotension, chest pain, heart failure or syncope), so managed in general practice with the supervisor. ED if any of these develop.
  2. Stroke prevention: CHA2DS2-VA 2, so oral anticoagulation with a DOAC (e.g. apixaban 5 mg twice daily) in preference to warfarin, and not aspirin (eGFR 75, Hb, platelets and INR checked; reduce alcohol and control BP rather than withholding it).
  3. Rate control for symptoms: a beta-blocker such as metoprolol, titrated to symptoms and resting heart rate.
  4. Investigations: repeat 12-lead ECG now to confirm sinus rhythm (and check PR and for pre-excitation); transthoracic echo; Holter or event monitor; fasting lipids and an absolute CVD risk assessment (Australian CVD risk calculator); replace magnesium.
  5. Risk factors: reduce or stop alcohol with support offered, checking for dependence or withdrawal risk before advising abrupt cessation (thiamine; supported withdrawal plan or AOD referral if dependent); quit smoking (Quitline 13 78 48), lose at least 10% of weight, exercise, BP control, nightly CPAP.
  6. Refer: cardiology for rhythm control (antiarrhythmics or ablation).

• Answer: this is not a heart attack. It is an irregular rhythm from the top chambers of the heart. The main danger is a clot causing a stroke, and a blood thinner greatly lowers that risk. His smoking, drinking, weight and BP still raise his heart attack risk, and tackling them also reduces the episodes; we will check his cholesterol and overall heart risk.
  • Beer: yes, cutting down is one of the most effective ways to reduce the episodes and the bleeding risk; offer help to cut down safely rather than stopping abruptly, and acknowledge it has been his way of coping.
  • Blood thinner: it does carry some bleeding risk, but for him the stroke risk without it is higher; cutting alcohol and controlling BP make it safer, and he should report any bleeding.
  • Call 000: face drooping, arm weakness, slurred speech; chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness, palpitations with dizziness.
  • On a blood thinner: black stools, vomiting blood, blood in the urine, or a head injury mean urgent care.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 1 to 2 weeks with the echo and monitor results, check HR, BP and the blood thinner, cardiology referral, carer support.

ddx.for: Sudden-onset, self-terminating, fast irregular palpitations now daily, an irregularly irregular pulse with a pulse deficit, an ECG with no P waves, a regular pulse after the episode stopped, and heavy alcohol, smoking, hypertension, OSA and obesity.
He describes his heart sometimes missing a beat.
ddx.against: Sustained fast episodes lasting minutes to hours, and the ECG shows a continuous irregular rhythm without P waves rather than isolated early beats.

ddx.dx: Atrial flutter with variable block or another supraventricular tachycardia
ddx.for: Episodes start and stop suddenly and are fast.
ddx.against: The rhythm he taps and the ECG are irregularly irregular, with no regular flutter waves.

ddx.for: His mother had thyroid problems, and hyperthyroidism is a classic AF trigger.
ddx.against: No weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor or goitre, and normal TSH and free T4.

ddx.for: Major stress and poor sleep since his wife's cancer diagnosis.
ddx.against: Objective irregular tachycardia on examination and ECG, and episodes come on at rest without worry.

ddx.dx: Ventricular tachycardia from underlying ischaemic heart disease
ddx.for: A 66-year-old smoker with hypertension and a father who died of a heart attack.
ddx.against: Narrow QRS complexes, no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting, and no ischaemic change on the ECG.

guide:
Part 1 is set at 09:20. Frank is in an episode at the time; reveal this only if the candidate asks whether he has the palpitations now, or when they feel his pulse. Give the alcohol quantity only if asked directly. Give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. Credit examination items 18–21 if the candidate names the system and the signs looked for; the examiner gives findings in one line each. Credit item 22 if the candidate asks for an ECG at any point in Part 1. For item 7, tick each cluster asked; the cardiovascular cluster is marked in item 6.

Part 2 is set at 15:45 the same day, after the episode has stopped on its own. Hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. The investigation marks (ECG, FBE, UEC, calcium, magnesium and phosphate, TFTs, TTE) are earned when the candidate interprets the bloods and ECG and plans the echo in question 3. Accept CHA2DS2-VASc or CHA2DS2-VA, as both give 2 here. Frank asks his questions during question 4 if they have not already been covered.

A high-performing candidate asks Frank to tap the rhythm, screens cardiac, thyroid and psychiatric causes and the PIRATES precipitants, quantifies the alcohol without judgement, and asks the stroke and bleeding history. They feel an irregularly irregular pulse and ask for an ECG straight away. In Part 2 they name paroxysmal AF, score it 2, start a DOAC, tackle the alcohol, smoking, weight and OSA, arrange an echo and refer to cardiology, and answer the heart attack question honestly.

A borderline candidate takes a generic cardiac history without establishing whether the rhythm is regular, misses the alcohol or the thyroid questions, does not calculate a stroke score, offers aspirin, or decides no anticoagulation is needed because he is back in sinus rhythm.
explain:
The diagnosis: paroxysmal atrial fibrillation

Frank has had fast, irregular palpitations for a couple of months. They start and stop suddenly, come on at rest and now happen every day. When he taps them out they are fast and irregular. In the clinic his pulse is irregularly irregular with a pulse deficit, and the ECG taken during symptoms shows no P waves, a fibrillatory baseline and an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at about 110. By the afternoon he is back in a regular rhythm without treatment; a repeat ECG confirms sinus rhythm. Episodes that stop on their own within 7 days are paroxysmal AF. He has many risk factors: heavy daily alcohol, a 30 pack-year smoking history, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, obesity, inactivity, recent major stress and his age.

Taking a palpitations history

Palpitations are often benign, but some carry a risk of serious cardiac or cerebrovascular events. Asking the patient to tap out the rhythm shows whether it is fast, slow or normal, regular or irregular. Ask how often episodes happen, how long they last, and how they start and stop. Then ask about red flags that may need ED: chest pain (angina), breathlessness and swelling (heart failure), and fainting or near-fainting. Low blood pressure in an episode also needs urgent care. Use cluster questions for the other differentials:

  • Cardiovascular: chest pain or tightness, breathlessness, fatigue, dizziness, syncope, nausea, sweating, ankle swelling.
  • Endocrine (thyroid): weight loss, increased appetite, heat intolerance, nervousness, sweating, diarrhoea, neck swelling.
  • Psychiatric: irritability, restlessness, poor sleep, poor concentration, excessive stress or worry.
  • AF precipitants (PIRATES): Pulmonary disease (including PE and pneumonia), Ischaemic heart disease, Rheumatic/valvular heart disease, Anaemia/Atrial myxoma, Thyroid, Ethanol (alcohol), Sepsis/Sleep apnoea. Electrolyte disturbance (potassium, magnesium, calcium) is a further trigger to check separately.

Risk factors for palpitations can be grouped as cardiac or non-cardiac, and reversible or irreversible. For AF they include smoking, alcohol, stress, obesity, OSA, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, coronary disease, valve disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, sepsis and electrolyte disturbance.

Interpreting the results

  • ECG: AF shows no P waves and irregularly irregular QRS complexes. A regular sawtooth pattern would suggest flutter, and a wide QRS would raise concern for VT or aberrant conduction. When the pulse becomes regular, a repeat ECG is recorded: a regular pulse of about 75 can also be atrial flutter with 4:1 block, so palpation alone does not confirm sinus rhythm. The repeat ECG also checks the PR interval and looks for pre-excitation, and gives a baseline in sinus rhythm before any antiarrhythmic.
  • FBE: looks for anaemia and for infection as a trigger. His macrocytosis fits alcohol.
  • UEC: looks for kidney disease and guides DOAC choice and dose.
  • Calcium, magnesium and phosphate: look for electrolyte triggers. His low magnesium should be replaced.
  • TFTs: exclude hyperthyroidism. They are normal.
  • LFTs: his raised GGT and transaminases fit heavy alcohol use.
  • Transthoracic echocardiogram: characterises any structural heart disease (LV function, valves, atrial size) linked to AF.

Stroke risk and anticoagulation

Once AF is found, take the history needed for a stroke risk score. Many references use CHA2DS2-VASc: Congestive heart failure, Hypertension, Age 75 or over (2 points), Diabetes, Stroke or TIA (2 points), Vascular disease, Age 65 to 74, Sex category. The NHFA/CSANZ 2018 Australian guideline uses CHA2DS2-VA, which leaves out sex. It recommends oral anticoagulation at a score of 2 or more and suggests considering it at 1. Frank scores 2 (hypertension and age), so anticoagulation is recommended. Paroxysmal AF carries a stroke risk like that of persistent AF, so being in sinus rhythm now does not remove the need. A DOAC is preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF; aspirin is not used for stroke prevention. Bleeding risk is lowered by tackling modifiable factors (alcohol, uncontrolled BP, NSAIDs) and is not a reason by itself to withhold anticoagulation. Check renal function, FBC and liver function before starting.

Rate, rhythm and risk factors

  • Stability first: hypotension, chest pain, heart failure or syncope means ED. Frank is stable.
  • Rate control: a beta-blocker or a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (diltiazem or verapamil, avoided if LV function is reduced) controls symptoms in episodes.
  • Rhythm control: antiarrhythmic drugs or catheter ablation are options for symptomatic paroxysmal AF; refer to a cardiologist.
  • Risk factor management: the Australian guideline recommends it as part of AF care, as it reduces AF burden. This means weight loss (aim at least 10%), alcohol reduction, smoking cessation, BP control, treating OSA and regular exercise. An Australian randomised trial showed that stopping alcohol reduced AF recurrence in regular drinkers. Frank drinks about 10 standard drinks a day (a middy of full-strength beer is about 1.1 standard drinks), far above the NHMRC guideline of no more than 10 a week and 4 on any one day. Assess dependence and withdrawal risk before advising him to stop, and offer support. Offer thiamine supplementation, and consider a supported withdrawal plan or referral to alcohol and other drug services if he is dependent.
  • Cardiovascular risk: his fear of a heart attack is reasonable. As a 66-year-old smoker with hypertension, he should have fasting lipids and an absolute cardiovascular risk assessment (Australian CVD risk calculator).
  • The whole person: his wife's cancer is a major stressor, and he is now a carer. Ask about his supports and offer help.

Safety netting

Teach the stroke warning signs (face drooping, arm weakness, speech difficulty) and to call 000 at once. He should also call 000 or go to ED for chest pain, fainting, severe breathlessness or palpitations with dizziness. On an anticoagulant, black stools, vomiting blood, blood in the urine or a head injury need urgent review. Review him in 1 to 2 weeks with the echo and monitor results, check his heart rate, BP and how he is tolerating the anticoagulant, and follow up the cardiology referral.
points: Ask the patient to tap out the palpitations: fast and irregular points to AF, fast and regular to SVT or VT, and a missed beat to ectopics.
Always ask about chest pain, breathlessness, fainting and near-fainting, and check BP; any of these with palpitations may need ED.
Screen cardiac, thyroid and psychiatric causes and the PIRATES precipitants; check FBE, UEC, calcium, magnesium, phosphate and TFTs, and arrange an echocardiogram.

Take the history for a stroke score in every patient with AF: CHA2DS2-VA of 2 or more means oral anticoagulation (a DOAC in preference to warfarin, never aspirin), whether the AF is paroxysmal or persistent.
Alcohol, obesity, smoking, hypertension and OSA drive AF; managing them reduces AF burden and is part of treatment, not an afterthought.
Bleeding risk is reduced by tackling modifiable factors such as alcohol and BP, not used on its own as a reason to withhold anticoagulation.
